analysis.body:
# Government AI Adoption and Implementation

Federal agencies are in the early stages of operationalizing AI, with the scope of deployment still heavily weighted toward planning rather than production use. According to GAO audits of federal AI use, twenty of twenty-three agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, but most of these remain in the planning phase. In about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases, with applications including analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies are using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets.

Implementation of AI governance requirements has proceeded unevenly across the federal government. Per GAO findings, ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from the requirements. Commerce and the General Services Administration took the lead by establishing specific AI infrastructure: Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence. By contrast, the Offices of Management and Budget and Personnel Management did not fully implement selected requirements. OMB has not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and OPM has not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. These gaps in centralized guidance mean that agencies cannot consistently manage AI deployment across the federal system.

Data quality and inventory accuracy remain significant challenges to effective AI management. GAO's analysis found that five agencies provided comprehensive information for their reported AI use cases while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories did not include required data elements such as the AI life cycle stage or an indication of whether an AI use case was releasable or not. Two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies to not be AI. Without accurate inventories, the federal government's ability to manage its use of AI and assess risks is hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

Internationally, government AI readiness is measured against multiple frameworks that assess policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks over 900 national AI policies and initiatives and has created an integrated partnership with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights provides cross-national comparison through the Government AI Readiness Index, which scores nearly every country on these dimensions. Both frameworks emphasize trustworthy AI systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure, and safe.

At the state level, regulatory activity is accelerating. As of the most recent tracking, 4,344 AI bills were tracked across 53 U.S. jurisdictions and updated daily from LegiScan. This legislative proliferation reflects growing government attention to AI governance but also creates potential fragmentation in how government entities at different levels are expected to acquire and deploy AI systems. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI, indicating federal commitment to AI capability building, though actual deployment remains nascent and fragmented without centralized acquisition and deployment guidance.
